title: Generic Stack Data Structure
story: You need a stack for integers, then a stack for strings, then a stack for game items. Writing three separate stacks is wasteful. One generic Stack[T] serves them all - push, pop, peek for ANY type.
why: Generic data structures let you write one implementation that works with any type, eliminating duplicate code and bugs.
analogy: A shelf bracket holds books, boxes, or toys - the bracket doesn't care what goes on it. Stack[T] is the bracket: same structure, holds anything. The T is just a placeholder for 'whatever you put here'.
try_it: Create a Stack[Float64] and push 1.1, 2.2, 3.3. Pop all three and print. Then create Stack[Bool] with true/false. Notice how pop() returns values in reverse order (LIFO).
tips: The `[T]` after struct name declares the type parameter
Each method must also declare `[T]` to use the generic type
pop() returns Option - None if empty, Some(value) if there was an item
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add [T] to method definitions: `fn Stack.pop[T]` not `fn Stack.pop`
Returning the item without removing it from the Vec
Not handling the empty stack case - always check len() == 0 first
